st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: OpenAI’s account supports the cluster’s core framing of Harvey as specialised infrastructure for complex, multi-step legal workflows while keeping lawyers in the review and client-service loop. Its reported growth and custom-model claims reinforce Harvey’s test-case status, although the evidence is promotional, largely founder-reported, and does not establish durable advantage, independent accuracy or broader effects on billing and leverage.
qs: This has allowed Harvey to deliver AI systems that help with tasks requiring complex reasoning, extensive domain knowledge, and capabilities beyond a single model call—such as drafting documents, answering questions about complex litigation scenarios, and identifying material discrepancies between hundreds of contracts.

st.an: OpenAI’s account supports the cluster’s principal proposition by presenting Harvey as a domain-specific workflow layer that applies custom models to complex legal tasks while keeping lawyers in a review and decision-making role. st.an: The source supports trusted, professional-facing use of legal AI, presenting Harvey as a supportive team member that handles routine work. Its vendor claim that the custom model avoids fabricated cases and grounds sentences in cited cases addresses reliability, although it does not examine verification costs, security governance or broader organisational safeguards.

The vision is for Harvey to serve as a supportive member of the team.

kp.k: AI synthesis shifts lawyers toward decisions and client work
kp.d: The OpenAI account presents Harvey as a platform that synthesizes information for lawyer review, helping with document drafting, complex litigation questions and identifying discrepancies across hundreds of contracts. Weinberg links this augmentation model to increasing transactional and litigation complexity; the proposed benefit is less time processing legal texts and more time making decisions and helping clients.
qs: They saw an opportunity to use LLMs to synthesize information and present it to lawyers for review.

"Both transactional work and litigation have been getting increasingly complex—there might be hundreds of thousands of contracts to go through for an international merger, and millions of emails to review for litigation," Weinberg explained.
With AI helping synthesize documents, lawyers can spend less time sifting through and drafting legal texts, and more time making decisions and helping clients.

kp.k: Early attorney feedback suggested usable landlord-tenant answers
kp.d: Weinberg reports an early exercise using GPT‑3 to answer landlord/tenant questions drawn from Reddit's r/legaladvice and sharing those answers with attorneys. For 86 out of 100 questions, attorneys reportedly said they would send the answer to a client without editing. This is reported attorney willingness to use the answers, rather than evidence of actual client delivery or outcomes.
qs: An early proof point came when Weinberg and Pereyra pulled Reddit's r/legaladvice for landlord/tenant questions and used GPT‑3 to generate answers, which they shared with attorneys.
"For 86 out of 100 questions, the attorneys said they would have just sent the answer to the client without editing," Weinberg said.

kp.k: Complex case research motivated custom training beyond retrieval
kp.d: Harvey initially tried public-API fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation for open-ended case law research but encountered limitations. Weinberg distinguishes simple retrieval answers from finding support for legal arguments. The account says foundation models had reasoning strengths but insufficient legal knowledge, motivating custom training to introduce both domain knowledge and ways of reasoning about it.
qs: They tried the obvious techniques first: fine-tuning foundation models via public APIs and building retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. But they ran into limitations with such a uniquely complex, open-ended use case.
"With case law research, you're finding ammo for your argument, and that's much more difficult to do."
So, Harvey decided to partner with OpenAI to build a custom-trained model that would allow them to inject new knowledge, and ways of reasoning about that knowledge, into base models.

kp.k: Custom development combined legal expertise with expanded case data
kp.d: Pereyra describes collaborative development involving Harvey lawyers explaining case law research, Harvey researchers sharing their work and OpenAI identifying technical approaches. The account reports that the project began with Delaware case law, expanded to all U.S. case law and added the equivalent of 10 billion tokens worth of data.
qs: "A lot of it was sitting down together, having our lawyers explain how case law research works, having our researchers show what we've done, and learning from OpenAI about the levers we had to approach the problem."
Harvey and OpenAI worked together to add the depth of context needed, first starting with case law from Delaware, and then expanding to include all of U.S. case law.
They added the equivalent of 10 billion tokens worth of data to power the custom-trained case law model.

kp.k: Lawyers reportedly preferred custom outputs over GPT‑4
kp.d: Harvey worked with 10 of the largest law firms, showing attorneys side-by-side outputs from its custom case law model and GPT‑4 answering the same question. Weinberg reports preference for the custom model 97% of the time, usually because answers were longer, more complete, more nuanced and covered more relevant case law. The reported measure is lawyer preference, not a separately stated accuracy score.
qs: To test the case law model, Harvey worked with 10 of the largest law firms.
They provided attorneys with side-by-sides of the output from the custom case law model, versus the output from GPT‑4 for the same question.
"97% of the time, the lawyers preferred the output from the case law model," Weinberg said.
"Usually, it was because it was a longer, more complete answer. It went into the nuance of what the question was asking and covered more relevant case law."

kp.k: Weinberg claims fabricated cases eliminated and sentence-level support
kp.d: The account identifies hallucination reduction as a motivation for custom training. Weinberg asserts that the model does not invent cases and that every sentence is supported by its cited case. This is a co-founder's claim carried by OpenAI, distinct from the reported lawyer-preference comparison.
qs: Hallucination reduction was one of Harvey's motivations for building a custom model, and the investment paid off.
"Not only does the case law model not make up cases, but every sentence is actually supported with the case it's citing," Weinberg said.

kp.k: Further applications include drafting and cross-jurisdictional research
kp.d: As rollout expands, Harvey describes prospective applications of its case law model in drafting briefs and motions and helping attorneys understand differences in case law between jurisdictions. These are applications the company is eager to explore, rather than reported findings from deployed use.
qs: As they roll this out to more users, Harvey is eager to explore other applications of the case law model, such as drafting briefs and motions, or helping attorneys understand how case law varies across different jurisdictions.

kp.k: Agents aim to reduce prompting and routine task burdens
kp.d: Harvey identifies agents as a next focus, described here as combining multiple model calls into one working output to simplify use and reduce prompt engineering and typing. Weinberg frames the vision as supportive of professionals: handling complex but routine tasks that occupy associates so professionals can spend more time on client interactions.
qs: One of their focuses is agents, or how to combine multiple model calls together into a single working output.
This would simplify the user experience and reduce the amount of prompt engineering and typing users need to do.
"The volume of legal work is growing and associates spend countless hours on complex, but routine, tasks," Weinberg said.
"The opportunity we have, not just with legal but with all professional services, is to take care of the routine tasks so professionals can focus their time on client interactions."

kp.k: Founders should anticipate improving model capabilities
kp.d: Pereyra recommends building for future rather than current model capabilities and tackling more complex versions of problems so that subsequent model improvements do not solve the product's target problem incidentally. This is strategic advice for AI founders, not an empirical finding about legal practice.
qs: "Don't build for the current capabilities of models today—build for where the models are going to be. Tackle more complex versions of problems so that when better versions of the models come out, they aren't solved as a side effect."

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: OpenAI and Harvey describe AI as augmenting lawyers by synthesizing and drafting legal material, enabling more time for decisions and clients.
pts.d: OpenAI states that Harvey's custom-model partnership supports complex reasoning, document drafting, litigation questions, and comparison of hundreds of contracts. The article frames these capabilities as supporting lawyers who review synthesized information, rather than replacing them. Harvey co-founder Winston Weinberg anticipates routine-task automation across professional services, allowing professionals to focus on client interactions.

pts.k: Harvey claims custom legal training enables more useful case-law research than basic retrieval or an uncustomized foundation model.
pts.d: Weinberg argues that retrieval alone handles simple legal questions but is less useful for the argument-building research attorneys need. OpenAI reports that foundation models had reasoning strengths but lacked the necessary legal knowledge, motivating custom training to add both knowledge and ways of reasoning about it. Weinberg attributes attorneys' preference for the resulting model to more complete answers, greater nuance, and more relevant case law.

pts.k: Weinberg claims the custom case-law model avoids fabricated cases and supports every sentence with its cited case.
pts.d: The article presents hallucination reduction as a motivation for custom training and reports Weinberg's categorical claim about the resulting model. This is a speaker-reported capability claim; the document does not supply a separate measured hallucination rate or citation-support test.

pts.k: OpenAI describes planned extensions into brief and motion drafting, cross-jurisdiction research, and multi-call agent workflows.
pts.d: These are prospective applications rather than reported completed deployments. The article says Harvey is exploring further uses of its case-law model and developing agents, described here as combining multiple model calls into one working output. The predicted user benefit is a simpler interface with less prompt engineering and typing. The source does not specify autonomous execution or removal of lawyer review.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article offers two attorney assessments: an early 100-question GPT-3 exercise and a custom-model comparison with GPT-4 involving 10 large law firms.
pts.d: Weinberg reports that attorneys would have sent GPT-3 answers to clients without editing for 86 of 100 landlord/tenant questions drawn from Reddit's r/legaladvice. Separately, OpenAI says Harvey worked with 10 of the largest law firms to compare answers from its custom model and GPT-4 side by side; Weinberg reports 97% preference for the custom model. The latter is a preference result, not a reported accuracy or hallucination rate. The article does not specify the comparison's question count, attorney count, blinding, or sampling procedure. Both exercises are reported within OpenAI's account of its partnership with Harvey.

pts.k: Technical-development experience and founder testimony support the account; the document does not quantify time savings or future workflow benefits.
pts.d: OpenAI reports unsuccessful or limited initial approaches using public-API fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation, followed by collaboration between lawyers and researchers and the addition of the equivalent of 10 billion tokens of data. These details describe the development basis for the capability claims, rather than a controlled estimate of their effects. Claims about time reallocation, agent usability, and future applications are presented as explanations or expectations without measured productivity outcomes. Harvey's reported revenue growth and fundraising provide company context, not evidence of legal-output quality.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2024 article distinguishes existing custom-model results from undated rollout ambitions and future agent development.
pts.d: The GPT-3 exercise is described as an early proof point, without a date. The custom-model partnership is described as recent and its comparison results as already obtained. Development began with Delaware case law and expanded to all U.S. case law, defining the stated legal coverage. Brief and motion drafting and jurisdictional comparison are framed as applications to explore during wider rollout; agents are a next focus, with no delivery deadline. Gabe Pereyra's advice assumes continued model improvement and recommends building for future rather than current capabilities.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are practicing lawyers, especially associates doing document-intensive work, and their clients; the broader vision includes tax and finance professionals.
pts.d: Transactional lawyers and litigators are presented as facing large volumes of contracts and emails. Associates are singled out for time spent on complex but routine tasks. Lawyers researching U.S. case law are the immediate users of the custom model, with large firms providing the reported comparison setting. Clients are expected to benefit from professionals devoting more attention to them. The landlord/tenant exercise concerns potential client-facing answers, but the source does not claim demonstrated access-to-justice outcomes. Harvey is described as a software platform for law, tax, and finance, not as an ALSP delivering legal services. No specific prediction is made about staffing reductions, fees, or employment displacement.
